turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'm the practice nurse. I'll check your blood pressure and temperature before the doctor sees you, if that's all right.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning. Yes, of course. Thank you.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): One hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-six, temperature thirty-six point seven. All quite steady.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): And the main problem today, so I can note it?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Pain in my lower back. It has been rather persistent.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm his wife. He's been moving very carefully at home.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, do come in. I'm Dr Shah. I've seen the nurse's readings. What can I help with?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I have pain across the lower back, and I thought it wise to seek advice.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry it's dragged on. When did it begin?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks ago, I would say. It came on gradually.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's been since we moved, and that was about two months ago. He's mentioned it on and off ever since.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The move was when it became noticeable, yes. I may have underestimated it as only a few weeks.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you say a few weeks, your wife says about two months, from the move. I'll record that range rather than a firm start date.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That is fair.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Where exactly is it, and how does it feel?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Across the lower back, a little more on the right. A dull ache, and it catches if I bend.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does it travel down either leg?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The boxes were the worst of it, if I may say. The stairs in the new house are narrow, and there were a great many boxes.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): The lifting is relevant, and I'll ask about work shortly. Does the pain go down the leg?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. It is chiefly the back.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then I won't call it a definite spread into the leg. It sounds uncertain.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Quite so.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): What makes it worse, and what helps?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Bending and lifting at work make it worse. Rest, and a hot water bottle in the evening, ease it somewhat.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): What sort of work do you do?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I am a warehouse operative. Manual handling for much of the day, with some paperwork at a bench.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They've offered lighter duties. He won't take them.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I do prefer to pull my weight, though I am trying to be careful.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or pins and needles in the legs or feet?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. The floor is cold, so my feet are often chilly, and I cannot be sure of anything more.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not a clear numbness, then. I won't record yes or no.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. That is accurate.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your bladder? Starting, leaking, or not knowing when you need to go?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My bladder has been entirely normal.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or feeling shivery?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The heating was off for the first fortnight after we moved. We sat about in coats. Most inconvenient.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, that does sound unpleasant. Have you actually had a fever, though?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. I have not had a fever.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight without trying?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): The kitchen was not finished, so meals were mostly sandwiches. I do not feel I have lost weight, but I have not been on the scales.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you can't really say, even though you don't think you look thinner?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Precisely. I would rather leave it uncertain than guess.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His clothes fit the same, as far as I can tell.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll leave weight loss as not established either way.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I appreciate you not pressing me to invent a figure.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in the legs, or pain that wakes you at night?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. It aches when I turn over in bed, but it does not wake me from sleep as such.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's tireder than usual, though he won't say so.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I am a little more tired, yes, with the move and rather poor sleep from turning. I would not call the tiredness severe.

[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me summarise the red flags. No bladder trouble, no fever, no leg weakness, and the pain does not wake you. Numbness, weight loss, and pain down the leg stay unclear, while the tiredness and poor sleep are mild. Is that a fair account?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. That is a fair summary.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): What painkillers have you used?

[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, one gram, up to four times a day, when it is troublesome. And ibuprofen. I believe it is four hundred milligrams, though I am not entirely certain of the strength. Twice a day, with food.
[SEG0054] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box at home is two hundred milligram tablets. He takes two, so I think that comes to the same thing. He often skips the evening dose.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I do miss the evening dose rather often. I should be more regular.

[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the intended ibuprofen dose is four hundred milligrams twice a day, but we haven't seen the packet, and evenings are often missed. Paracetamol one gram, up to four times daily, as needed.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I can check the box at home.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else you take regularly?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, five milligrams, once each morning, for my blood pressure. I have been on it for several years.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): High blood pressure is still an ongoing problem, and you are still taking the amlodipine?
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. It is generally well controlled.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have no allergies that I am aware of.
[SEG0064] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had a rash with penicillin years ago. They told him not to take it again.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not altogether sure that was a true allergy. It was a long time ago. I have avoided penicillin since, all the same.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll record a possible penicillin rash as disputed, not confirmed. Your wife recalls advice to avoid it, and you are unsure.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems the sensible course.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any previous operations?
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any old tests I should know about, for the back or otherwise?
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Not for the back. About three years ago my GP did a cholesterol blood test, and they said it was borderline. I was not given a number.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): Borderline cholesterol on a blood test about three years ago, no figure given, and no imaging of the spine. I won't enter that as a definite cholesterol condition.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Quite right. Borderline was all they said.
[SEG0074] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father had a bad back and had surgery for it later in life.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): That is true. My father did undergo surgery for his back.
[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): Noted as family history only. Do you smoke, or drink?
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. A glass of wine with Sunday lunch is the extent of my drinking.
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll examine your back now, if you can stand.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly.

[SEG0080] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tender over the lower lumbar area, slightly more on the right. Flexion is reduced. Straight leg raise is clear on both sides. Power and sensation in the legs are normal, and you do not look feverish.
[SEG0081] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that spot on the right is the tender one.

[SEG0082] person_4 (DOCTOR): Overall, this is low back pain for somewhere between a few weeks and about two months, aggravated by bending and lifting in warehouse work, eased by rest. I think this is most likely mechanical low back pain. I can't entirely rule out an early disc irritation, given the vague comment about the leg, but nothing today suggests a serious cause.
[SEG0083] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Thank you for explaining it so carefully.

[SEG0084] person_4 (DOCTOR): Continue the paracetamol, one gram up to four times a day. Carry on with ibuprofen four hundred milligrams twice a day with food, if your stomach is comfortable, and please try not to miss the evening dose.
[SEG0085] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I can do that.
[SEG0086] person_4 (DOCTOR): Check the packet so we know the strength. I might arrange an MRI if this has not settled. Let's see you again in two weeks.
[SEG0087] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall. Should I bring the ibuprofen box next time?

[SEG0088] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, please bring it. Reception will book the two-week appointment. If bladder trouble or true leg weakness appears before then, come back straight away rather than waiting.
[SEG0089] person_2 (PATIENT): I will. Thank you again, Doctor.
[SEG0090] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll see that the box goes in his bag.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
